questions.question: What are wrapper classes in Java and why do they exist?
questions.title: Wrapper Classes
questions.direct_answer: Wrapper classes (Integer, Double, Boolean, etc.) wrap primitive types into objects, required for use in collections and generics which can't hold primitives.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of primitives vs objects and Java's type system
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing the primitive-to-wrapper mappings or forgetting char→Character, int→Integer (not Int)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the Number class hierarchy and useful static utility methods

sections.standard_example: Java 17 app processing user input and generating reports

beats.content: Java collections — ArrayList, HashMap, HashSet — can only hold objects, not primitives. Wrapper classes solve this by wrapping each primitive type in an object: int becomes Integer, char becomes Character, and so on.

Common mistake: int→Integer, not Int→Integer. And char→Character, not Char→Character. Beyond enabling collections, wrapper classes provide static utility methods used constantly in algorithms: Integer.parseInt(), Integer.MAX_VALUE, Integer.compare(), Integer.bitCount().

sections.hook: Collections can't hold primitives. Wrapper classes bridge that gap — and bring a set of utility methods that come up in almost every algorithm problem.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
So Java has two kinds of types: primitives (int, double, boolean, char, byte, short, long, float) which are fast raw values with no methods, and objects. The problem is that Java's collections — ArrayList, HashMap, HashSet — can only hold objects, not primitives. And generics like List<T> only work with object types.

Wrapper classes bridge this gap. Each primitive has a corresponding wrapper class: int→Integer, double→Double, boolean→Boolean, char→Character, byte→Byte, short→Short, long→Long, float→Float. Integer and Double extend Number which extends Object.

Beyond making primitives usable in collections, wrapper classes provide useful utility methods: `Integer.parseInt(String)` converts String to int, `Integer.MAX_VALUE`/`Integer.MIN_VALUE` give the bounds, `Integer.toBinaryString(n)` converts to binary, `Integer.compare(a, b)` compares two ints safely, `Integer.bitCount(n)` counts set bits — all very useful in algorithms.

Since Java 5, autoboxing and unboxing handle the conversion automatically most of the time.

questions.question: What is the difference between Integer.parseInt() and Integer.valueOf()?
questions.title: parseInt() vs valueOf()
questions.direct_answer: parseInt() returns a primitive int; valueOf() returns an Integer object (and uses the Integer cache for values -128 to 127).

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of parsing and the Integer cache
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using parseInt() when you need an Integer object for a collection, or not knowing about the caching behavior
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the Integer cache (-128 to 127) and its == implications

sections.standard_example: Java 17 app processing user input and generating reports

beats.content: Both parse a String to a number. The difference is the return type — and that difference has a subtle consequence.

rows: Yes — reuses cached objects for -128 to 127

beats.content: The cache trap: Integer.valueOf(100) == Integer.valueOf(100) returns true — same cached object. Integer.valueOf(200) == Integer.valueOf(200) returns false — outside cache range, two different objects. Always use .equals() to compare Integer values. Use parseInt() when you need a primitive; use valueOf() when you need an Integer object for a collection.

sections.hook: parseInt and valueOf both parse strings to numbers. But only one of them can return the same object twice — and that creates an == trap.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
So parseInt() takes a String and returns a primitive int. valueOf() takes a String (or int) and returns an Integer object.

The key difference beyond return type is the Integer cache. `Integer.valueOf(n)` for values between -128 and 127 returns a cached Integer object — the same object every time. So `Integer.valueOf(100) == Integer.valueOf(100)` returns true because they're the same cached object. But `Integer.valueOf(200) == Integer.valueOf(200)` returns false because 200 is outside the cache range and creates new objects each time.

This is a famous Java gotcha. When you autobox an int to Integer in a collection, values in that range reuse cached objects — which is fine for equality checks with .equals(), but causes surprising == behavior.

Practical rule: use parseInt() when you want a primitive int (most common case). Use valueOf() when you need an Integer object or want the caching behavior. Use .equals() not == to compare Integer objects.

sections.title: Key Points
content: parseInt() → primitive int
valueOf() → Integer object
Integer cache: -128 to 127 returns same cached object
valueOf(127) == valueOf(127) → true (cached)
valueOf(200) == valueOf(200) → false (new objects)
Always use .equals() to compare Integer objects

questions.question: What are Integer.MAX_VALUE and Integer.MIN_VALUE and where are they used?
questions.title: Integer Bounds
questions.direct_answer: Integer.MAX_VALUE is 2^31-1 (2,147,483,647) and Integer.MIN_VALUE is -2^31 (-2,147,483,648) — used as initial values when finding max/min and for overflow detection.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Hardcoding 999999999 instead of Integer.MAX_VALUE, or using Long.MAX_VALUE for int arrays
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show why Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1 overflows to Integer.MIN_VALUE

sections.standard_example: Java 17 app processing user input and generating reports

beats.content: Integer.MAX_VALUE is 2 to the 31 minus 1 — that's 2,147,483,647. Integer.MIN_VALUE is negative 2 to the 31 — that's -2,147,483,648. These are the largest and smallest values a Java int can hold.

content: Classic algorithm use: int max = Integer.MIN_VALUE; then iterate and update with Math.max()
Or: int min = Integer.MAX_VALUE; iterate and update with Math.min()
Overflow trap: Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1 wraps around to Integer.MIN_VALUE
For sums that might overflow: use long, or Math.addExact() which throws on overflow
Don't hardcode 999999999 — Integer.MAX_VALUE is the correct sentinel

sections.hook: Every min/max algorithm needs a starting value. Integer.MAX_VALUE and MIN_VALUE are Java's built-in sentinels — use them instead of hardcoding magic numbers.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Classic use: int min = Integer.MAX_VALUE; for(int n : arr) min = Math.min(min, n)
Overflow trap: Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1 = Integer.MIN_VALUE (wraps around)
For large sums: use long or check for overflow with Math.addExact()

questions.question: What useful methods does the Character class provide for string processing?
questions.title: Character Class Methods
questions.direct_answer: Character.isDigit(), isLetter(), isUpperCase(), isLowerCase(), toUpperCase(), toLowerCase(), isWhitespace() — essential for character-by-character string validation and parsing.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Manually checking c >= '0' && c <= '9' instead of Character.isDigit(c)

sections.standard_example: Java 17 app processing user input and generating reports

beats.content: The Character class has static utility methods for testing and converting individual characters. Use them instead of manual range checks — they're more readable and handle Unicode correctly.

content: Character.isDigit(c) — true for '0' to '9' and Unicode digits
Character.isLetter(c) — true for a-z, A-Z and Unicode letters
Character.isLetterOrDigit(c) — combined check, useful for alphanumeric validation
Character.isWhitespace(c) — space, tab, newline, form feed
Character.toLowerCase(c) / toUpperCase(c) — single character case conversion
Character.getNumericValue('7') returns 7 — cleaner than '7' - '0' for digit extraction

sections.hook: Writing c >= '0' && c <= '9' manually is error-prone and doesn't handle Unicode. Character.isDigit(c) is one method call that does it right.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Character.isDigit(c) — true for '0'-'9' and Unicode digits
Character.isLetter(c) — true for a-z, A-Z and Unicode letters
Character.isLetterOrDigit(c) — combined
Character.toLowerCase(c) / toUpperCase(c) — single char case conversion
Character.isWhitespace(c) — space, tab, newline, form feed
Character.getNumericValue('7') → 7 (for digit parsing)

questions.question: What is the Number class hierarchy in Java?
questions.title: Number Class Hierarchy
questions.direct_answer: Number is an abstract class extended by Integer, Long, Double, Float, Byte, Short, and also BigDecimal and BigInteger — providing intValue()/doubleValue() conversion methods.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing BigDecimal and BigInteger also extend Number
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that Number enables writing methods accepting any numeric type: void process(Number n)

sections.standard_example: Java 17 app processing user input and generating reports

beats.content: Number is an abstract class in Java that all numeric wrapper types extend. It defines four conversion methods that every numeric type must implement: intValue(), longValue(), floatValue(), and doubleValue().

content: Primitive wrappers that extend Number: Integer, Long, Double, Float, Byte, Short
High-precision types that also extend Number: BigDecimal, BigInteger
Concurrent types: AtomicInteger and AtomicLong also extend Number
Practical use: a method that accepts Number works with any numeric type — void process(Number n)
Narrowing warning: ((Number)bigDecimal).intValue() silently loses the decimal part

sections.hook: Most candidates know Integer and Double extend Object. The deeper answer is they all extend Number — including BigDecimal and BigInteger.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Number abstract methods: intValue(), longValue(), floatValue(), doubleValue()
Primitive wrappers: Integer, Long, Double, Float, Byte, Short
Also extends Number: BigDecimal, BigInteger, AtomicInteger, AtomicLong
List<Number> can hold any numeric type (useful for generic code)
Narrowing conversion: ((Number)bigDecimal).intValue() — loses precision
